newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish president says U.N. rights job "daunting".
newsitem.headline: Irish president says U.N. rights job "daunting".

text.p: Ireland's President Mary Robinson said on Friday her appointment as United Nations Commissioner for Human Rights was "a daunting task".
"It is a daunting task to take on principal responsibility for human rights on behalf of the United Nations," the 53-year-old president told an Irish conference on refugees.
Speaking the day after the announcement of her appointment, Robinson said her new job would require a new understanding between the world's rich and poor countries.
"There will need to be bridges built between developing countries and the developed world, a need to listen and a need to stand up at times with courage," she told delegates.
She pledged she would try to stay in touch with non-governmental organisation (NGOs) with whom she has worked to bring aid and support to the less privileged both in Ireland and the developing world.
"I would hope to keep very closely in touch with those who work at the coal face, the many NGO's who work in the area of human rights," she said.

Robinson was making a chacteristic speech against racism and in support of sympathetic treatment of refugees, an issue which has grabbed front page Irish headlines because of a sudden increase in the number of asylum seekers.

She said Irish history should help shape attitudes towards the hundreds of East Europeans and Africans seeking asylum in Ireland because of the two million who sought refuge in the United States during the Irish famine 150 years ago.
"If our mind is right, if our approach is right, if we are true to our own story, our own history, we will do it right," she told delegates.

Robinson said racism is "rearing its ugly head in many countries" and warned that there were signs it could reappear in Ireland itself, traditionally a country of welcome for the homeless and the exiled.

Newspapers have focused on the arrival of hundreds of East Europeans, principally Romanians, whom police believe were smuggled into Ireland to take advantage of social security benefits and allowances.
"If we are not very careful, it could lead to an emergence of racism, which is so contrary to our own life story," she said.
